CO2016B-P1-1.exp: An analog computer operates directly on continuously varying physical quantities such as voltage, pressure or shaft rotation, so the input is never digitised at all. Options A and C describe a digital or hybrid machine, not a pure analog one.

CO2016B-P1-2.exp: Artificial intelligence is the defining feature of the FIFTH generation, and that option is simply not printed here, so the question has no strictly correct answer. Fourth Generation is the closest of the four because the microprocessor era is where AI work first became practical; treat this as a defective item.

CO2016B-P1-3.exp: First-generation machines (ENIAC, UNIVAC, roughly 1940-1956) switched using vacuum tubes and valves. Transistors mark the second generation and integrated circuits the third, which is the usual trap on this question.

CO2016B-P1-4.exp: The Arithmetic Logic Unit performs all arithmetic and logical operations inside the CPU. The Control Unit only decodes instructions and directs traffic; it does no arithmetic itself.

CO2016B-P1-5.exp: A CPU is made up of the Arithmetic Logic Unit and the Control Unit (plus its internal registers). RAM and ROM are main memory sitting outside the CPU, so options B and C confuse memory with processor.

CO2016B-P1-6.exp: A hard disk gives the fastest retrieval of the three because it spins fast and supports direct (random) access. Magnetic tape is strictly sequential and the slowest, and a floppy is far slower and lower-capacity than a hard disk.

CO2016B-P1-7.exp: Addressing always starts at the lowest location, 00000(16), and runs up to the top of the addressable range, so 00000 to 9FFFF is the only option with a valid starting address. The other three begin partway in, leaving locations below them unaddressable.

CO2016B-P1-8.exp: A logical operation (AND, OR, NOT, or a comparison) yields only true or false, i.e. a Boolean value. Arithmetic operations, by contrast, return numeric results.

CO2016B-P1-9.exp: A register is built as a group of flip-flops, one flip-flop storing one bit, so an n-bit register needs n flip-flops. Gates perform combinational logic but cannot hold a value, which is why options A and B fail.

CO2016B-P1-10.exp: The address bus is unidirectional: the CPU always drives the address out to memory and I/O, and nothing sends addresses back. The data bus is the bidirectional one, and mixing the two up is the standard trap here.

CO2016B-P1-11.exp: The status register holds individual condition bits (carry, zero, sign, overflow) that are called flags, hence its alternative name flag register. The accumulator is a data register and the stack is a memory structure, so neither is an alias for it.

CO2016B-P1-12.exp: Memory here means primary/RAM, which loses its contents at power-off and is therefore temporary, while storage means disk or other secondary media that retain data permanently. Option C inverts a different distinction: memory is faster than storage, not slower.

CO2016B-P1-13.exp: RAM is volatile: cut the power and its contents vanish. ROM and EPROM (printed here as EPROME) are non-volatile by design, which is exactly why the boot firmware lives there.

CO2016B-P1-14.exp: EEPROM expands to Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory, erasable in place by applying a voltage. The near-miss distractors substitute Easily or Electronic for Electrically.

CO2016B-P1-15.exp: RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost the moment power is removed, which rules it out for permanent storage. RAM is in fact the fastest and most compact of the storage tiers, so the speed, reliability and bulk options are all wrong.

CO2016B-P1-16.exp: Access time is defined as the average interval between issuing an address and having the data available. Seek time is only the head-positioning component on a disk, and transfer time is the separate period spent actually moving the bytes.

CO2016B-P1-17.exp: All three statements describe the same underlying justification for caching: programs exhibit locality of reference, references cluster in address space and time, and the 90-10 rule is the rough empirical form of that observation. Picking only one of them misses that they are restatements of each other.

CO2016B-P1-18.exp: Cache sits between the CPU and main memory (RAM), holding recently used blocks so the processor is not stalled by slower DRAM access. The CPU never talks to the hard disk directly, so option C describes the wrong pair of levels.

CO2016B-P1-19.exp: Of the four properties listed, lower power consumption is the only genuine advantage DRAM has over SRAM; its one-transistor-one-capacitor cell also makes it denser and cheaper per bit. Needing refresh circuitry is a drawback, DRAM is slower than SRAM, and its cell density is higher, not lower.

CO2016B-P1-20.exp: 8K bytes of main memory needs 13 address bits (2^13 = 8192), and fully associative mapping stores the entire address as the tag alongside the data, so each cache word is 13 tag bits + 8 data bits = 21 bits. The trap is forgetting the tag and counting only the data byte.
